items.title: Pakistan Agricultural Research Council suspends officers over ‘recruitment irregularities’
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Agricultural Research Council (PARC) has suspended several officers over their alleged involvement in irregularities in the organisation’s recruitment process, senior officials of the Ministry of National Food Security and Research informed a Senate committee on Tuesday. The officials told the Senate Standing Committee on National Food Security and Research that an inquiry under the Efficiency and Disciplinary Rules had also been initiated against the officers. The committee was further informed that the matter was currently sub judice. The meeting, chaired by Senator Syed Masroor Ahsan, was attended by Senator Poonjo Bheel and Senator Sardar Al Haj Muhammad Umer Gorgaij. The committee expressed serious concern over the failure to submit the required written reply and relevant record concerning the alleged recruitment irregularities. Members also discussed the plight of candidates who had applied for PARC vacancies but were now approaching the upper age limit. The committee recommended exploring a mechanism that would allow such candidates to participate in future PARC recruitment drives even if they subsequently exceed the prescribed age limit, in order to protect their interests. Members also stressed that the prescribed provincial quota must be implemented across all posts, including lower-grade positions. Officials said the required codal formalities for implementing the provincial quota had been completed and assured the committee that the quota would be enforced. The committee was also briefed on the National Oilseed Policy and the country’s growing edible oil import bill. Officials said the federal government was planning measures to increase domestic oilseed production, with particular emphasis on olive cultivation. Senator Ahsan expressed concern over the challenges confronting domestic edible oil production and called for practical steps to boost local output. He directed the ministry to submit a comprehensive report covering progress made over the past three years, PSDP projects, initiatives related to olive oil production and future plans to increase domestic oilseed production.­ Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Constituency issues dominate NA session
items.description: • Deputy speaker defers entire 58-point agenda, including 20 private members’ bills • PPP legislator demands policy statement from PM on new provinces • MNAs voice concern over rise in violence against women ISLAMABAD: It was a largely non-productive and wasteful day in the National Assembly on Tuesday as lawmakers spent nearly three hours raising petty issues, mostly related to their constituencies, under the guise of “points of order”. Deputy Speaker Ghulam Shah showed great generosity by allowing more than three dozen members to speak on issues of their choice, after announcing that the day’s entire legislative agenda had been deferred under an agreement. The deputy speaker, however, didn’t elaborate on where and with whom the understanding had been reached. Later, Aliya Kamran of the opposition Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) complained that her party was not consulted at all. The deputy speaker deferred the entire 58-point agenda, which included 20 private members’ bills. The House, however, took up the two calling attention notices — one related to the high fees and charges being collected by private medical colleges and the other regarding persistent river erosion in Layyah district — besides unanimously passing a resolution to mark Eid Miladun Nabi. Under the assembly rules, a member may raise a ‘point of order’ only to point out some violations during the proceedings and generally, the chair doesn’t allow the members to raise irrelevant issues under points of order. Taking advantage of the free rein given by the chair, the members spoke on all kinds of issues, ranging from matters of national importance to the problems relating to their constituencies. Interestingly, no government representative was there to respond to or take note of the points raised by the members. Most of the issues highlighted by the lawmakers were related to the provincial governments or the local governments that were not functioning. PTI lawmakers also talked about their constituency issues, but after protesting against the government’s alleged failure to implement the Supreme Court’s verdict regarding medical check-up of former prime minister Imran Khan at Shifa International Hospital, Islamabad. The speeches of the opposition members were completely blacked out on the official social media accounts of the National Assembly. Injustice to Sindh Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan and PPP legislators mostly criticised the federal government over long and frequent power outages in Karachi and other parts of Sindh. Another PPP MNA Sharmila Faruqui highlighted the alleged contradiction in the federal government’s development priorities, stating that while “the government repeatedly cites lack of fiscal space, it has approved Rs49bn in federal financing for the first phase of Lahore-Sahiwal-Bahawalnagar Motorway.” On the other hand, she said, the government had released only Rs30bn for the long-delayed strategic Hyderabad-Sukkur Motor­way, terming it a great injustice to the Sindh province. Highlighting some recent incidents, including the murder of Hina Javed in Rawalpindi, some lawmakers expressed serious concerns over the increase in violence against women in the country. Babar Nawaz and Shaista Khan of the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) referring to the murder of five-year-old Ayat Noor in Haripur, lashed out at the PTI-led provincial government, questioning the alleged silence of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and other party MPAs over the incident. The MNAs asked the KP government to take notice of the incident and bring the culprits to justice. New provinces PPP lawmaker Agha Rafiullah demanded that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif should come to the House to give a policy statement on the issue of new provinces. Referring to a statement by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, the PPP MNA from Karachi alleged that a cabinet member had charge-sheeted his own government by declaring that the system had collapsed in the country. On the other hand, PML-N lawmaker Babar Nawaz said the people of Hazara didn’t want to live under the present set-up and they wanted to have a separate province. He also claimed that historically, Hazara, Chitral and Swat had never been part of KP. The National Assembly will now meet on Friday at 11am. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Pakistan sits on $7tr mineral trove, claims planning minister
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has claimed that Pakistan estimates its mineral endowment at more than $7 trillion. Mr Iqbal made these remarks in a conversation with Farwa Amin, director for South Asian initiatives at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York, as per a statement issued by the planning ministry on Tuesday. The minister said large-scale mining operations required heavy up-front investments and extensive gestation periods, and the country’s volatile political climate was a primary deterrent to international resource developers. He said that with improved macroeconomic stability, the government was actively courting foreign partners, including US firms, through mechanisms such as the memorandum of understanding with US Strategic Metals, potential EXIM financing and participation in critical-minerals ministerial processes. Indus Water Treaty Mr Iqbal said India unilaterally held the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, describing it as the “first instance” in modern history of water being weaponised and creating a serious new security challenge for Pakistan. He said the 70-year-old treaty had remained “untouchable” even through multiple wars between the two countries. He warned that India could now deny Pakistan water when it was needed for crops and release it when it was not required, turning a shared resource into a potential instrument of pressure. He said Pakistan was accelerating construction of new reservoirs to create a strategic buffer, adding that the Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand dams, once completed, would add roughly six million acre-feet of storage capacity. These projects are intended both to stabilise water supply against climate-driven variability and to reduce vulnerability to upstream manipulation, he said, adding that Islamabad was pursuing diplomatic channels to prevent the dispute from escalating into conflict. He also placed geoeconomics at the centre of Pakistan’s foreign policy under the “Uraan Pakistan” framework and the 5E strategy, arguing that the relationship with the United States in particular must move beyond the traditional security-geopolitics axis. Ties with US, China Mr Iqbal was equally clear that en­­gagement with the US would not come at the expense of China. He described China as a “trusted partner” that stepped in during Pakistan’s energy crisis with the first phase of the CPEC, delivering approximately $25 billion in investment that ended prolonged power shortages and upgraded highways, fibre-optic networks and Gwadar Port. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Fresh efforts at mediation revive hopes for US-Iran climbdown
items.description: COMMERCIAL vessels are seen in the Strait of Hormuz, near the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas, as Tehran and Muscat agreed on a phased arrangement for the troubled waterway. According to the two sides, the agreement covers the formation of a temporary joint navigation corridor, mine clearance, information exchange and traffic management.—Reuters • Back-to-back Tehran trips by CDF Munir, Omani FM yield progress on key issues • Despite public brinkmanship, Washington ‘ready to show flexibility’ on economic sanctions if Iran meets ‘certain conditions’, US media reports • Diplomatic sources point to ‘softer than expected’ sanctions, say Islamabad taking the lead in conveying messages from Tehran to Washington, and vice versa • Iran seeks return to terms agreed in Islamabad MoU; eyes Hormuz agreement with Oman ISLAMABAD / WASHINGTON: Progress made during two key visits to Tehran — by Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir and Omani Foreign Minister Badr Al-Busaidi — may have opened the first potentially workable pathway towards de-escalation in the Gulf, since the breakdown of the armistice secured through the Islamabad Memor­andum of Understanding (MoU). Although there has been no clear breakthrough yet, and fundamental differences persist between Iran and the United States, the latest diplomatic activity has brought the political and technical dimensions of the dispute back into focus. In Washington too, there seems to be a willingness to consider sanctions relief as part of a broa­der understanding with Tehran, provided Iran meets certain conditions. According to some US media reports, Washington has offered an end to economic sanctions and the naval blockade against Iran in exchange for Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping and halting attacks by Iran-aligned regional groups. However, the specific terms have not been publicly confirmed by Washington or Tehran. Importantly, unlike the period following the collapse of the June understanding, when the two sides were largely talking past each other and the crisis was bec­o­ming increasingly militarised, there is a renewed push towards establishing a new mechanism for maintaining the ceasefire. Observers believe Field Mars­hal Munir’s visit served to reopen channels bet­w­­een Tehran and Washington, through Islamabad. It is also noteworthy that the Iranian reaction to the visit was unusually positive, with Seyed Mehdi Tabatabaei, deputy for communications and information at the Iranian president’s office, describing it as “highly fruitful” and saying it had produced “highly valuable diplomatic achievements”. The CDF’s meeting with Gen Mohsen Rezaei — the Supreme Leader’s representative on the Supreme National Security Council – was particularly significant in testing whether the security side in Tehran was also prepared to join the renewed process. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), too, said the Iranian leadership appreciated Pakistan’s “constructive role and sincere efforts” for dialogue and de-escalation. But Tehran has so far not publicly indicated any readiness to make unilateral concessions to US, rather, the message emerging from the meetings was that Iran remains prepared to return to the understanding formalised under Islamabad MoU, provided Washington first addresses what Tehran considers its violations of the memorandum, and returns to implementing the understanding. ‘Softer than expected’ sanctions Diplomatic sources in Washington also confirmed that Pakistan’s mediation role is being supported from the top, with Field Marshal Munir remaining in touch with both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, complemented by working-level contacts between US and Pakistani officials. Asked whether Pakistan had conveyed any US proposals to Iran, sources confirmed that this was the case, adding that Tehran’s proposals have also been relayed to Washington, “along with their comments”. “So, they are not only facilitating but also [carrying out] mediation, which includes conveying their opinions as well,” sources said. The description is broadly consistent with reporting by CBS News and The Wall Street Journal , both of which have identified Pakistan as an important conduit between Washington and Tehran. As evidence of the impact this messaging is having on the Trump adm­in­­istration’s actions, diplomatic sources in Washin­gton pointed to the recent announcement of economic sanctions against Iran. Although the Trump administration had billed the sanctions as spelling an “ economic doomsday” for Tehran, diplomatic sources said: “The restrictions are softer than expected, and also, on the other side, there have been no recent attacks on Gulf states”. While the Treasury Department has announced new sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels, but the list did not feature any of the Chinese financial institutions thought to be facilitating Iran’s oil trade. The Iranian position, nevertheless, remains conditional as it continues to regard the Islamabad MoU as the appropriate framework, but wants Washington to demonstrate through concrete action that it is prepared to honour its commitments. The dispute over Hormuz is, meanwhile, not being treated by Iran as a separate maritime issue rather it has been tied to the issues of sanctions, the US naval blockade and reciprocal implementation of the June understanding. Hormuz progress In this context, the progress made in Oman-Iran talks assumes greater significance. Al-Busaidi’s visit to Tehran produced some forward movement on navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, with the two sides agreeing on a phased arrangement. As per the joint statement, the understanding between Oman and Iran includes a temporary joint navigation corridor, mine clearance, information exchange and traffic management, while technical discussions would continue on a permanent navigation arrangement. Al-Busaidi said in a post on X after the meeting that he hoped the countries would “soon announce” the temporary corridor in the strait. “Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course,” he said. Technical negotiations will continue to determine a “permanent navigational corridor and future administration of the Strait, as well as a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services”, the earlier joint statement read. The announcement came as US President Donald Trump repeated claims on Truth Social that “all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz”, citing the US navy. “Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed… There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in full force and effect,” he added. Meanwhile, the Reuters news agency reported that Washington is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran. The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Govt increases petrol price by Rs1.12, high-speed diesel by Rs1.11
items.description: Pakistan fuel prices, 2026 Official ex-depot prices (PKR/litre) — OGRA & Ministry of Energy notifications Petrol (MS-92) Diesel (HSD) Pre-crisis baseline Source: OGRA / Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division); Dawn.com · "> The government on Tuesday raised the price of petrol by Rs1.12 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.11 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs343.10 per litre while HSD will cost Rs371.80 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to a Petroleum Division notification, the new prices will be applicable on Aug 26 (Wednesday) and 27 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: France permanently closes consulate in Karachi
items.description: KARACHI: The Consulate General of France in Karachi is closing its doors permanently after 50 years of service. This was announced by the outgoing French Ambassador to Pakistan Nicolas Galey at a farewell organised by the Board of Management of the Quaid-i-Azam House Museum in collaboration with the Karachi Council of Foreign Relations on Tuesday. The event was aimed at saying goodbye to two great friends of Pakistan: Ambassador Galey and the Consul General of France in Karachi Alexis Chahtahtinsky. The ambassador said that he was also feeling a bit sad after spending almost five years in Pakistan. Farewell held for French Ambassador Nicolas Galey and Consul General Alexis Chahtahtinsky “And my leaving is also coinciding with the departure of our Consul General in Karachi Alexis Chahtahtinsky. Someone will replace me in Islamabad but here in Karachi, the French Consulate, which opened in 1976, is closing down after 50 years of service,” he said. “I have visited Karachi many times and have seen the vitality of this city. I have seen it changing and improving,” he said, while appreciating Consul General Alexis for his good work in Karachi. “Even though the consulate is closing, there is still the Alliance Francaise, which will now serve as our flagship. There will also be the Pakistan France Business Alliance here doing its work,” the Ambassador reminded. He also said that he really appreciates Pakistan’s efforts in at least getting “a kind of ceasefire in the Gulf. Pakistan has emerged as a very influential country in difficult circumstances.” Consul General Chahtahtinsky said that he was leaving Karachi and Pakistan on September 1. “I am going back to France but I am taking great memories of Karachi with me,” he said, adding that he is not just a great friend but also an old friend of Pakistan. “I first visited Pakistan as a student in 1983, which was a great thing, because as a diplomat you don’t get so much freedom to go where you want. I was lucky enough to visit and fall in love with the Northern Areas of Pakistan at the time,” he said. “As the Consul General, I spent another four memorable years in Karachi, which was the first capital of Pakistan and still its economic hub. Indeed, Karachi, as the biggest port in the country, is the gateway to Pakistan,” he said. “It is a great place for doing business and has a great social life. I will always have a special place in my heart for Karachi,” he added. “Earlier Pakistan had a reputation of crime and terrorism and embassy people used to be afraid to come here. But since February 28, when the major conflict erupted in the Gulf, Pakistan has also emerged on the world map due to its mediation efforts. The entire world is grateful to Pakistan for its role. It is a very different Pakistan that we are leaving. Instead of being a problem, Pakistan has repositioned itself to become part of the solution,” the consul general said. During his vote of thanks, Vice Chairman of the Board of Management of the Karachi Council of Foreign Relations Ikram Sehgal recounted that France was the first non-Muslim nation to recognise Pakistan though diplomatic relations between both countries were established in 1951. “France has lent Pakistan support whenever we needed it. We got Daphne-class submarines followed by the Agosta-class submarines at a time when no one was giving us weapons. “Before that we had the Mirage III and Mirage 5 fighter jets. Through Project Retrofit of Strike Element [ROSE], a modernisation programme for ageing Mirage jets carried out at the Pakistan Aeronautical Complex in Kamra, we are still flying their upgraded versions. In between, we also captured some French army tanks used by India to put into use ourselves,” he said, adding that France is wrong in closing its consulate in Karachi at this time when Pakistan’s waters are turning into a major power. “This is a time when France could have taken advantage of the opportunities coming up here in the name of trade and new alliances are coming up geopolitically as Pakistan gets ready to play a big role,” he concluded. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Indepe­ndent power producers found overcharging users through costly coal procurement
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Indepe­ndent power producers (IPPs) operating on impor­ted coal have been found imposing an additional burden on electricity consumers through opaque and inefficient coal procurement practices, with the cost ultimately passed on through monthly fuel price adjustments (FPAs). While consumer groups have been raising concerns over such practices at various forums, including public hearings, the power division and the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) have now also pointed to inefficiencies in coal procurement and their financial impact on consumers. The issue gained prominence after recent competitive bidding for coal supply to the 660MW state-owned Jamshoro Power Plant attracted a discount of $7.12 per tonne from a Karachi-based supplier compared to discounts of only 20 to 50 cents per tonne in some contracts involving IPPs. “The power division has identified significant inefficiencies in the procurement of imported coal by power plants,” an official statement said on Tuesday, adding that fresh policy guidelines had been iss­ued “for corrective action that could save the natio­nal exchequer up to Rs380 million annually”. In a recent order, Nepra had already pointed out concerns over coal procurement by Port Qasim Electric Power Company (PQEPC) under a six-year contract involving discounts of $0.20 to $0.50 per tonne based on estimated coal prices. “This type of evaluation has never been observed in any bidding by any other power plant, including PQEPC, and does not seem justified, as it is based on estimated coal prices, which may change in future,” Nepra said in its judgement. The regulator also noted that the Port Qasim plant had published its tender notice only in China instead of reaching out to a broader pool of potential bidders. “Had discounts been incorporated into the bid evaluation as a major criterion, it may have yielded more competitive and higher discounts from prospective bidders,” Nepra said. The regulator also observed that the plant had not disclosed that it had already executed a long-term coal supply agreement when the matter was discussed with the regulator on two occasions, prompting “proceedings regarding misstatement and/or non-disclosure of information”. Nepra subsequently directed the Port Qasim plant to conduct fresh bidding for a long-term coal supply agreement within three months of its March 2026 FPA decision. However, officials said that after the March 25 order, the company procured about 1.2 million tonnes of coal, enough for almost an entire year, just before a new tender. They said the contract again involved a discount of around $0.50 per tonne against the $7.12 discount secured by the public-sector Jamshoro plant. The difference alone works out to around $8 million, officials said. If similar procurement practices were followed by other IPPs, the impact could rise substantially. The power division said the procurement inefficiencies were identified during a series of meetings presided over by the power minister, where officials reviewed actual data, contractual arrangements and market practices. “Pakistan has a significant fleet of coal-fired power plants with a combined capacity of approximately 5,280 megawatts that rely wholly or partly on imported coal. These include three major 1,320MW plants at Port Qasim, Hub Power and Sahiwal, as well as the Lucky and Jamshoro plants which also have the capability to use imported coal,” it said. The division said coal import prices for IPPs were linked to internationally recognised benchmarks such as the API-4 index, but the final price paid by a plant also depended on the discount negotiated with the supplier. PQEPC Chief Financial Officer Adil Ashraf and Procurement Chief Liang Ding Ping did not respond to Dawn’s written queries. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: How close are humanoid robots to becoming part of our everyday life?
items.description: At the ongoing 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games, multiple robots have clocked times better than human benchmarks in sprint and other track‑and‑field events, marking rapid progress in humanoid‑robot technologies. Industry observers on site note that while competitions showcase the cutting‑edge technical capacity of today's robots, real‑world everyday applications remain in the early phase. Robots are gradually moving beyond exhibition‑only competition demos toward practical deployment in real‑life scenarios. One industry participant at the games pointed out that this edition brings notable new milestones. For the first time, robot competitive results are measured against human performance benchmarks, proving robots can outperform humans under specific controlled conditions. Unlike earlier competitions that largely focused on basic locomotion, this year's event features a wide range of autonomous operation challenges — an important step toward broader industrial adoption. Still, competition‑level performance does not automatically translate into viable mass‑market consumer products. Pain points and limits uncovered during matches can drive further technical iteration. Meanwhile, non‑humanoid robotic alternatives, such as wheeled platforms fitted with robotic grippers, also hold considerable practical application potential. Kang Yu, general manager of the Capital Markets Department at Shoucheng Holdings, shared her observations on industry investment trends. Against a backdrop of surging investor interest in robotics, many industry players are prioritizing long‑term foundational‑technology R&D rather than chasing short‑term market hype. Investment spans multiple links across the robotics value chain: robot hardware, joint materials, embodied‑intelligence models, computing infrastructure and data. A key focus lies in boosting product reliability and consistency, with further improvements expected to come as production scales up. The public listing of Unitree Robotics represents a meaningful capital‑market turning point for the sector. It highlights value‑driven technology as a core underpinning for the industry's long‑term growth outlook. Experts tracking real‑world robot deployment said physical‑world testing spaces in Beijing's commercial districts, transport hubs and office complexes now display over 200 types of intelligent hardware, with use‑cases covering home companionship, education and healthcare. Industry projections suggest robot costs could drop substantially over the next three years. As algorithms keep advancing, robots may eventually evolve into mass‑consumer goods. Deploying robots within real‑world use‑cases will be central to how the industry moves forward.

items.title: CIA chief visits Moscow, media reports
items.description: US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, CBS News reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. It would be the first known visit to the Russian capital by a US intelligence chief since Ratcliffe's predecessor, William Burns, held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in November 2021. The Russia visit also appears to be Ratcliffe's first as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with his Russian intelligence counterparts, according to the report. Ratcliffe's visit comes as US-mediated efforts to end the Ukraine crisis remain largely stalled, with Moscow and Kiev still far apart on key issues. Neither Washington nor Moscow has so far confirmed the visit. (With input from agencies)

items.title: 'Not an enemy:' Slovakia calls on EU for 'friendly' China competition
items.description: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly" competition with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers. Fico made the remarks after talks in Bratislava with European Council President Antonio Costa, who began his annual tour of EU capitals in Slovakia. Fico said Slovakia was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally, arguing that greater competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to do better and outperform others. "I have a different view about relations between the EU and China. I don't think we should fight China by putting up barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to do better." The two leaders' discussions also covered the EU's next long-term budget, competitiveness, energy prices and enlargement. On the EU budget, Fico said Slovakia supported maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc. "We're even saying that some extra funding should be found for countries in the eastern part of the EU, which, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said, adding that a strong agricultural policy is another key Slovak priority. On an EU enlargement, Fico reiterated Slovakia's support for countries seeking membership, adding that all applicants must meet the required criteria. "That means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And that also applies to Ukraine," he stressed. Fico said Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, arguing that they had been preparing for EU membership for much longer. (With input from Xinhua)

items.title: Trump Plans to Buy Midterm Ads About His Own Record
items.description: P resident Trump gathered his top political advisers in the Oval Office early this month to solve a problem of riches: how to spend his super PAC’s $400 million political war chest with fewer than 100 days to go before the midterm elections. Republican strategists are concerned about Trump’s low approval ratings and voter anxiety about the economy. One person familiar with the Oval Office strategy meeting put it this way: “When the issues that you typically campaign on don’t move voters—or voters are pissed off at you about those issues—the question becomes: What do you campaign on?” Some GOP strategists favor focusing entirely on specific races in an effort to convince voters of the merits of individual candidates and local issues. But Trump himself has rejected that approach. House and Senate Democrats, the president noted during the meeting, will make their fall campaigns a referendum on him. His advisers told him that the poor polling reflects the fact that the voting public still does not know about many of his accomplishments—the dozens of new stock-market highs, a decline in fentanyl deaths, the “sealed” southern border, the increase in domestic-manufacturing production. The solution Trump settled on, according to three people familiar with the meeting, was to lean into the Democratic strategy of focusing on himself. The president ordered a series of television advertisements about his own record that will serve as a backdrop to the hundreds of individual House and Senate contests. Trump wanted what one person described to us as “environmental lift” ads—commercials that would focus on nationalizing the midterms broadly around his victories—and he suggested that the ad makers mine his own on-camera statements as building blocks. “Go look at the clips,” the president told his team, according to this person. “I cite accomplishments all the time.” That decision has resulted in a Trump midterm-election ad blitz that is set to be rolled out soon from MAGA Inc., the main repository of Trump’s political fundraising, according to people familiar with the discussions, all of whom insisted on anonymity to describe internal conversations. Most of MAGA Inc.’s spending is still expected to go to targeted House and Senate races, for which the group has been establishing teams to review polling, voter modeling, and message testing. “We are going to unload the guns on both chambers real soon,” one of the people said. But another person told us that because Trump will inevitably be part of voters’ considerations, highlighting his achievements makes sense. “I think everybody does understand that the president and his agenda are on the ballot to some degree,” another person told us. A spokesperson for MAGA Inc. told us that the group does not comment on internal deliberations or plans. Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told us that Trump is committed to maintaining the Republican majorities in Congress. “President Trump is cleaning up Joe Biden’s mess,” she said in a statement. “There is a great story to tell because the United States of America has never been stronger than under his leadership.” Trump’s decision to focus a portion of his spending on himself echoes President Biden’s decision in the fall of 2023 to launch a series of ads trumpeting his own legislative record, as he sought to increase his approval rating in advance of his reelection bid. But Trump is not on the ballot this fall, which presents new risks. A new strategy of touting Trump’s achievements could well backfire by aiding Democratic efforts to make each race about national issues at a time when Trump’s approval rating is at record lows. Yet given the midterm headwinds, Republicans may have little choice but to present their most effective communicator to voters. T he political climate —an economic election in which voters don’t feel that their life has gotten better, despite some positive indicators—is in many ways similar to what Democrats faced in 2010 and 2022, when the electorate blamed their party for the economic pain of the 2008 financial crisis and the coronavirus pandemic, respectively. But in other ways, the situation Trump faces is different. Polls show that voters aren’t just anxious about inflation; they are frustrated with Trump’s war of choice with Iran and concerned about government corruption. Before Trump’s first midterm election as president, in 2018, the Pew Research Center found that 51 percent of the country believed that the economy was doing well, including 13 percent who described the economy as excellent. By July of this year, only 22 percent felt that the economy was doing well, and only 3 percent described it as excellent. Trump’s economic approval rating hovered at about 50 percent in 2018 public polls. Most polls this year show that his standing has fallen into the 30s. Republican political consultants have voiced concerns both publicly and privately in recent weeks about the triumphant tone of some of Trump’s economic messaging. Democrats see a familiar dilemma. “You’ve got to take voters from where they are to where you want to go, and the only way to do that is to not dismiss in any way what they know—and what I mean by that is, you can’t go in playing ‘It’s Christmas Time’ when that’s the last holiday they can afford,” Rahm Emanuel, who worked for the Obama and Biden administrations and is a potential contender in the 2028 presidential election, told us. “They’re going to put you on mute.” In 2010, Barack Obama wrestled with this problem by alighting on a “car in the ditch” metaphor to explain why, after the 2008 financial crisis, the promised recovery still felt slow in coming. Yet even that formulation proved ineffective, Obama’s senior strategist David Axelrod told us. “We sort of abandoned it because what we found was even that was offensive to people, because it felt like we were trying to blame others,” he said. “What we learned very quickly is, you cannot jawbone people into feeling what they do not feel in their own lives, and Biden defied that to his own detriment.” Trump has shown much more interest in hyperbole than in complicated metaphors, branding his second term in office as a new “Golden Age.” While stumping last Friday for Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, Trump spoke glowingly about his second term. “You have record manufacturing and auto plants being built right now in the United States and in South Carolina,” he said. “We have the greatest economy in our history. Now, some people haven’t seen it yet, but they will.” Axelrod noted that Trump argued at the same rally that his own polling “should be at 100 percent on the economy.” “If you’re the average person out there, you’re seeing that and thinking What planet is he living on? ” Axelrod said. “You have to acknowledge that people are struggling and this is a work in progress.” David Winston, a Republican strategist who works with congressional leadership, told us that key to the midterms is whether voters, when they walk into a grocery store, feel that they can manage at least a little bit better than before Trump returned to office. “So Republicans need to be talking about what actions they took in terms of the economy to at least get things moving in the right direction, and what the outcome has been,” he said. “This is one where it can’t be a laundry list of 35 talking points. This has to be one or two key things.” [ Read: How Trump left America vulnerable to cyberattacks ] Trump’s advisers are hoping to drive home a discrete set of facts about his accomplishments over the past 19 months. The list is likely to include new tax breaks for certain workers and seniors, the stock market’s rise over the past two years, the military’s boat strikes purportedly targeting fentanyl, and his efforts to “seal” the U.S.-Mexico border, to name a few. Rather than distance himself from congressional elections—the preference of some Republican candidates in swing districts—Trump has argued that he can drive turnout in those races by making himself the center of the conversation. Next month, he will host the Republican Party for a two-day “midterm convention” rally in Dallas aimed at nationalizing the November races as a choice between extreme Democrats and Republican accomplishments. Trump has asked his supporters to treat November as though his name is on the ballot. “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” Trump said on Friday in South Carolina. “Just say that I’m on the ballot one more time.” I n other, important ways, Trump is better positioned than either Obama or Biden were at this point in their midterm races. He has a massive cash advantage, thanks to his aggressive fundraising over the first year of his term that collected tens of millions from crypto companies, AI entrepreneurs, and traditional Republican donors. He also enjoys a sharply gerrymandered political map in the House that has created a new cushion of Republican-leaning seats after mid-cycle redistricting. And the Senate majority will be decided by races in Republican-leaning states such as Texas, Alaska, Ohio, and Iowa. Trump’s advisers have not yet indicated to Republican consultants how much money the president will spend on the midterms, according to people familiar with the matter. But the merits of Trump inserting himself into the election may be less important to some Republicans than the fact that MAGA Inc. is starting to spend. Some in the party have worried for months that Trump might hoard his fundraising for the 2028 presidential-election cycle—or for something else entirely. MAGA Inc. has begun work on a number of campaigns about specific House and Senate races for the fall. Much of that advertising is expected to feature negative attacks on Democratic candidates, the traditional role of independent super PACs. MAGA Inc. has commissioned polling and research, along with modeling in the targeted House and Senate races. It has also shared information with other independent groups, including the Senate Leadership Fund and the Congressional Leadership Fund, which are affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota and Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana. In the early spring, Trump’s aides hoped to launch a disciplined sales pitch to voters focused on Trump’s accomplishments, only to have that effort largely derailed by the open-ended Iran conflict. Trump’s approval ratings have eroded further since then. Now is the president’s last chance for a do-over, and his team is projecting confidence that it can get it right. “Anybody that is saying we are headed for a shellacking absolutely can’t just read the numbers,” one of the people familiar with the Oval Office meeting told us. With early voting starting in the first weeks of October, Republicans are once again betting that more Trump is their best way to block Democratic hopes of a wave election.
